Hormuz as Hostage

Iran just turned the Strait of Hormuz into a live “off” switch for Trump’s miracle peace deal. 

Tehran’s Khatam al‑Anbiya command announced the strait is closed again, accusing the US of breaking its own memorandum by failing to stop Israel from violating the Lebanon cease-fire. 

One night of rocket swaps and airstrikes on southern Lebanon — and the world’s main oil artery gets shut in revenge.

On paper, the US‑Iran preliminary deal was simple: end fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon, restart talks in Switzerland, slowly reopen Hormuz. 

Israel and Hezbollah traded volleys within 24 hours of the last truce, seven Lebanese civilians were reported killed, dozens wounded, and Tehran claimed this “clear breach” justified closing the waterway again. 

The “secondary front” in Lebanon has become the main veto power over the entire war’s endgame.

Washington insists the show goes on. Pakistan says “technical talks” will start Sunday at Bürgenstock; JD Vance tells Fox News his envoys — Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff — are already in Switzerland and ready to bargain, and Iran’s foreign ministry says its team is en route. 

But while diplomats talk about “discreet and reliable” Swiss hospitality, the only thing that really matters for markets is this: ships that had just begun moving more freely through Hormuz are now staring at headlines about closure — again.

Even inside Iran’s system, no one wants to own this mess outright. New supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei is already distancing himself from Trump’s memorandum, signaling that any final deal — billions in unfrozen assets, sanction relief, nuclear limits — can still be blamed on “the negotiators” if it turns sour. 

For Trump, it’s worse: his “decisive victory” over Iran now depends on Hezbollah fighters on a Lebanese ridge not shooting too much and the IDF not bombing too aggressively. That’s not hegemony. That’s crisis management by people who lost the remote.

So Hormuz is closed, again — not by storms or pirates, but by a political tantrum built into the deal’s DNA. One side bombs Iran for months, the other side shuts the oil gate every time its Lebanese proxies and Israel clash, and both then pretend they’re inching toward “permanent peace.” 

The war is supposedly ending, but the most important chokepoint on the planet just became the bargaining chip of a government that Washington swears is “finished.”

Trump’s Holy Deal: Bomb First, Bill Later

Trump didn’t “flip” on Iran. He just moved from phase one — outsourced bombing — to phase two: cashing in on the ruins. In this logic, Israel plays the attack dog, Gulf monarchies pay for reconstruction, and America sits on top like an East India Company with better branding.

From 2023 to 2026, Washington sketched a three‑step doctrine: Project 2025 blesses Israel and crushes Iran on paper, NSS 2025 pretends the Middle East is already “solved,” and NDS 2026 names Israel a “model ally” while quietly downgrading the whole region under Western Hemisphere priorities. None of these texts bothered to explain how to end a war — because endless pressure is the model. Exit strategy is not a bug. It’s heresy.

Inside the US right, two religions wrestle over the joystick. The dispensationalist crowd wants Israel to “take it all” for the glory of the End Times — for them, any deal with Iran is betrayal. The America First nationalists don’t care about prophecy; they care that Iran is defanged, trade routes are secured, and the US can declare victory without dying in another forever war. Trump plays to both: green‑lights strikes, then signs a deal once Tehran is weaker and the logistics map looks promising.

That’s the core of “delegated order.” Israel gets to hit Iranian infrastructure, DP World gets a 30‑year concession in Tartus, corridors like IMEC and the Syria–Turkey line open for business, and Gulf royals bankroll reconstruction in exchange for “security guarantees.” The threat is degraded, the shipping lanes are monetized, the map is rewired — and only then does Trump step out with the paperwork, calling it peace. 

For Israel, the message is brutal: you are a “model ally,” not God’s board of directors. You can fight, expand influence and redraw your immediate neighborhood — but you don’t decide when the US stops the war and starts doing deals. For Iran, the subtext is worse: once your nukes and regional muscle are knocked down, Washington prefers you alive, sanctioned and manageable — a neutered state that signs away its program so America can say, “Problem solved,” retroactively justifying what its own doctrine wrote years earlier.

In that sense, Trump’s Iran deal isn’t a glitch in his hawkish persona. It’s the point. Use delegated violence to break the threat, then freeze the new reality in place with a signature and a payment plan. The bombs speak in Israel’s language, the ports and corridors earn in Gulf and corporate language — but the "victory" decree always comes out in English, out of Washington.
